newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices steady as markets take stock.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices steady as markets take stock.

text.p: Buoyant world oil markets paused to take stock on Friday after a week spent shedding some of the heady gains sparked by Iraq's military confrontation with the United States.
London November futures for international benchmark North Sea Brent crude were trading 10 cents down on the day at $21.81 a barrel at 1652 GMT, off last week's peak of $24.30.
Traders on Friday were weighing an easing of Middle East tensions against unusually low inventories of heating oil in the United States and Europe approaching winter.

"The fireworks in the Gulf seem to be over for the time being, but the upshot is we've lost Iraqi exports for the forseeable future and refiners are struggling to cover stocks," said a trader with a major European oil company.
Iraqi exports, expected eventually to resume after a six-year break under a U.N. oil-for-food arrangement, are on hold following Baghdad's incursion into its northern Kurdish safe havens.
OPEC producers are set to enjoy a $26 billion export revenue windfall as a result of prices which already are averaging $2 a barrel more than last year.

"OPEC's in for a much-needed increase in revenues because we don't see much chance of oil prices coming down during the remainder of the year," said Leo Drollas, chief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) in London.
But oil traders in Europe on Friday sounded a note of caution over bullish oil price forecasts for the rest of the year.
Demand for West African crude sales into Asia in October has slumped after heavy purchases over the previous three months, leaving more crude available for U.S. and European refiners.
"There's a stubborn overhang of prompt crude supplies in the Atlantic Basin at the moment," said a European trader.
Oil analysts nevertheless have been busy over the past two weeks revising up price forecasts in the expectation that Brent won't go much below $20 before the end of the year.
They argue that crude stocks, at three to four days of world demand below year-ago levels, are likely to remain tight.
Seasonal refinery maintenance this autumn is scheduled much lighter than in previous years, keeping demand for crude buoyant.
The Paris-based International Energy Agency said recently it expected just 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) of U.S. refinery maintenance between September and November, less than half of last year.
European refinery shutdowns were likely to reduce crude demand by 430,000 bpd compared to 800,000 bpd last year.
